title: The week after running a marathon: Effects of running vs elliptical training vs resting on neuromuscular performance and muscle damage recovery
authors: Martinez-Navarro I, Montoya-Vieco A, Hernando C, Hernando B, Panizo N, Collado E
population: 64 road marathon finishers (54 men, 10 women; 39 +/- 4 years; finish time 3 h 35 min +/- 21 min), randomised at the finish line
findings: Randomised to running (RUN), elliptical (ELIP) or rest (REST). RUN and ELIP exercised continuously for 40 min at moderate intensity (95-105% of the heart rate at the first ventilatory threshold) at 48, 96 and 144 h after the marathon.
Lactate dehydrogenase and creatine kinase were sampled the day before, within 15 min of the finish and at 24, 48, 96, 144 and 192 h: no 'Intervention' or 'Intervention x Time' effect (p > 0.05).

Authors conclude that return to running at 48 h post-marathon does not seem to have a negative impact on muscle damage recovery up to eight days post-race and could be recommended to speed up neuromuscular recovery.
limitations: Marathon only, mid-pack recreational runners finishing in about 3.5 h; the running dose was a fixed 40 min at about first ventilatory threshold, three sessions; squat jump was the only functional outcome; not applicable to 50 km and longer races; no check-in or soreness gating was tested.
implications: Supports allowing easy running from about 48 h after a marathon: a run of up to about 40 min at or near first-threshold heart rate (conversational) on days 2, 4 and 6 did not slow CK/LDH recovery and was associated with better squat-jump recovery at 96 h. A fixed 7-day full stop after a marathon is more conservative than this evidence requires.
The result does not extend to 50 km, 100 km or 100 miles; keep the longer holds for those distances.
Use as the evidence for the 'easy and short, intensity-capped' shape of the marathon return, not for any quality session in the first week.
